t: Minimum Amount of Damage Dealt to Bob
o:
## Understanding the problem

Every second, ALL living enemies deal their damage to Bob, then Bob hits one living enemy for `power`. Enemy i needs tᵢ = ceil(health[i]/power) seconds of focused fire to die. Minimize the total damage Bob takes.

Example 1 (power 4): t = [1,2,2,2] for health [4,5,6,8]. Killing in order 3,2,0,1 gives 20+12+3+4 = 39. Example 3: one enemy with t = ceil(59/8) = 8 seconds, dealing 40/sec → 320.

This is a classic single-machine scheduling problem: each 'job' i occupies tᵢ seconds during which its own damage dᵢ (and all not-yet-killed enemies' damage) accrues. By an exchange argument, killing enemies with higher damage-per-second-to-kill (dᵢ/tᵢ) first is optimal: swapping adjacent out-of-order pair (i then j) to (j then i) changes total damage by dⱼ·tᵢ − dᵢ·tⱼ, which is an improvement exactly when dᵢ·tⱼ > dⱼ·tᵢ.
k: Enemy i needs tᵢ = ceil(health[i]/power) consecutive seconds; while killing it, every still-living enemy (including i) damages Bob each second.
Exchange argument: adjacent swap improves cost iff dᵢ·tⱼ > dⱼ·tᵢ, so sort by dᵢ/tᵢ descending (compare via cross-products to avoid floats).
Simulate the sorted order: answer += (remaining total damage) × tᵢ, then subtract dᵢ from the remaining total.

a.n: Approach 1: Smith-rule greedy ordering + linear simulation
a.i: Once the kill order is fixed, total damage is determined: processing kills in sequence, each kill i contributes tᵢ × (sum of damage of all enemies killed at or after i). Sorting by damage density d/t descending minimizes the weighted completion-time sum (Smith's rule), proven locally by the adjacent-swap inequality above.
s: Compute tᵢ = (health[i] + power − 1) / power for each enemy.
Sort indices so that dᵢ·tⱼ > dⱼ·tᵢ puts i first (cross-product comparator, all integers).
Walk the order maintaining rem = Σd: ans += rem·tᵢ; rem −= dᵢ. Return ans (up to ~10¹³, use 64-bit).

c.python:
class Solution:
    def minDamage(self, power: int, damage: List[int], health: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(damage)
        t = [(h + power - 1) // power for h in health]
        import functools
        idx = sorted(range(n), key=functools.cmp_to_key(
            lambda i, j: damage[j] * t[i] - damage[i] * t[j]))
        rem = sum(damage)
        ans = 0
        for i in idx:
            ans += rem * t[i]
            rem -= damage[i]
        return ans

a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the simulation pass is O(n).
a.sp: O(n) for the time array and index permutation.

w:
## Wrap-up

Recognize the weighted-completion-time structure: jobs = enemies, processing time = seconds to kill, weight = damage per second. Smith's rule (sort by weight/processing-time descending) is the answer; prove it with the adjacent swap rather than asserting it. Pitfalls: forgetting the dying enemy itself deals damage during its own tᵢ seconds (rem includes dᵢ when accumulating), floating-point comparators (use cross-products), and 32-bit overflow of the answer. Follow-up: enemies that heal, or Bob dealing variable damage per second.
